card.title: Academic vocabulary across 20 units — collocation is king

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Twenty units, one language spine: each theme (technology, ecology, power, migration…) deposits its academic word-stock — and NEB tests words the way adults use them, in COLLOCATION (make a decision, take responsibility, raise awareness), confusable pairs (economic/economical, historic/historical, sensible/sensitive) and contextual gap-fills. Knowing a word means knowing its neighbours, its register and its grammar (countable? which preposition?).

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: word knowledge = meaning + collocation + register + grammar  ·  confusables: economic (financial) / economical (thrifty) · historic (momentous) / historical (of history) · sensible (wise) / sensitive (touchy)  ·  collocation frames: make/take/have/do + noun (no logic — memorise pairs)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Collocations are conventional, not logical (heavy rain but strong wind) — exposure beats rules. Register decides synonyms (kids vs children vs offspring across casual/neutral/formal). Gap-fill answers must fit grammar AND sense AND collocation simultaneously.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Technology unit: 'artificial intelligence poses ethical questions' (poses, not asks). Ecology: 'raise awareness', 'combat climate change'. Power/politics: 'wield influence', 'abuse power'. Migration: 'flee persecution', 'seek asylum' — verb-noun pairs that examiners lift straight into blanks.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Attack an unknown word in four passes: (1) sentence context → rough sense; (2) word parts (eco+logy, migr+ation); (3) collocation memory (which verbs hug this noun?); (4) register check (formal essay vs chat). Four passes turn recognition into production — the actual NEB demand.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: No synonym is exact (slim/skinny/thin diverge in connotation). Lists memorised without contexts decay within weeks — spaced retrieval through the units beats cramming. Dictionary first-meanings mislead (check the field label: law? medicine? computing?).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: From corpus linguistics: words co-occur non-randomly (mutual-information scores prove it), so examinations test the high-MI pairs — 'commit a crime', not 'do a crime'. Learning one unit's theme deeply (say, ecology's raise/combat/preserve set) transfers the METHOD to all twenty units.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: MCQ options: kill by part of speech, then collocation, then sense. Confusable drills in pairs (economic/economical, historic/historical). Keep a theme-wise collocation diary — ten pairs per unit × twenty units = exam-proof vocabulary.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB-style: confusable-pair MCQs; collocation gap-fills from unit themes; synonym/antonym production; contextual word-attack on unseen lines.
